shoppers tend to overestimate the sales tax they will owe at the register and therefore buy less than they otherwise would.
excise taxes cost shoppers more than sales taxes of the same rate, since excise taxes are collected before goods reach the shelf.
items.explanation: Shoppers pay a sales tax and an excise tax of the same size either way, yet they cut back more when the tax appeared in the posted price, and they bought less once shelf tags showed the tax. The difference lies in whether the tax is visible on the tag, so shoppers seem to underweight taxes that are added only at the register, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The comparison in the study is between two kinds of tax, not between alcohol and other goods, and the shelf-tag result involved other products too.

C.why_wrong: If shoppers overestimated the register tax, adding it to the price tag would not lower sales; the results point to shoppers paying too little attention to that tax, not too much.

D.why_wrong: The text compares increases of comparable size; the stronger response to excise taxes comes from where the tax appears, not from its costing more.

sources.what: Chetty, Looney, Kroft 2009, American Economic Review, 'Salience and Taxation: Theory and Evidence': posting tax-inclusive price tags reduces demand by 8 percent; increases in taxes included in posted prices reduce alcohol consumption more than increases in taxes applied at the register

items.notes: Area: social science (public economics). S6: a tax in the posted price changes behavior, an equal tax added at the register does less, so visibility matters. Distractors: CMP (alcohol vs other goods), REV (overestimate), MIX (cost vs visibility).

review.source_checked: AEA abstract (Chetty, Looney, Kroft 2009): tax-inclusive price tags cut demand 8 percent; taxes in posted prices cut alcohol consumption more than taxes added at the register

band7.why: Two steps (equal taxes, unequal response; the difference is visibility); D keeps the excise contrast with a wrong cause, B and C partly plausible. Band 6.

items.subtype: T4 explanation by elimination: where the metal came from and how it was worked
items.passage: Small iron beads discovered in a cemetery at Gerzeh, Egypt, were manufactured around 3200 BCE, long before iron smelting is known to have been practiced anywhere. Before smelting, metallic iron was obtainable only from meteorites, which arrive on Earth already in metallic form and are typically far richer in nickel than iron extracted from ore. Examining one of the beads, archaeologist Thilo Rehren and colleagues determined that it was nickel-rich and had been made by repeatedly hammering a fragment of iron into a thin sheet and rolling that sheet into a tube, suggesting that the beads’ makers ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: obtained iron by smelting ore on a small scale and hammered it into shape because they did not yet know how to cast it.
chose meteoritic iron over iron smelted from ore because the nickel in meteoritic iron made it easier to hammer into thin sheets.
knew that their iron had come from a meteorite and valued the beads more highly for that reason.
shaped iron that was already metal when they obtained it, working it into a bead without first having to extract it from ore.
items.explanation: No one is known to have smelted iron that early, and the bead is rich in nickel, as iron from meteorites typically is, so the metal most likely came from a meteorite. Meteorites arrive already as metal, and the bead was hammered from a fragment, so its makers shaped iron they found in metallic form instead of extracting it from ore, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The beads predate any known iron smelting by more than a thousand years, and their nickel content matches meteoritic iron rather than iron smelted from ore.

B.why_wrong: The beads were made long before anyone is known to have smelted iron, so their makers had no smelted iron to choose against, and the text says nothing about nickel making iron easier to work.

C.why_wrong: The nickel and the hammering show where the iron came from and how it was worked, which researchers can now measure; they reveal nothing about what the makers knew of its origin or how much they valued the beads.

sources.what: Rehren et al. 2013, Journal of Archaeological Science: nine Gerzeh beads of about 3200 BC hammered from pieces of meteorites rather than iron ore (high nickel, cobalt, phosphorus, germanium), hammered into thin sheets and rolled into tubes, long before iron smelting

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology (archaeometallurgy). S4: only two sources of iron metal; smelting ruled out by date and by nickel content, so meteoritic; a meteorite arrives as metal and the bead was hammered from a fragment, so no extraction. Avoided the official 'Barring the possibility' frame. Distractors: REV (small-scale smelting, needs the date and the nickel), MIX (chose meteoritic over smelted iron, keeps nickel and sheets), EXT (makers knew and prized the meteoritic origin, keeps the meteorite). Key paraphrased off 'meteorite' and 'hammering'.

fixes: read easier than band 6 (B traders from smelting regions and C casting each died to one stated fact; key echoed 'meteorite' and 'hammering'): B rebuilt as choosing meteoritic over smelted iron for its nickel (keeps meteorite, nickel and sheets, breaks on timing), C as an overreach to the makers' knowledge and values, key paraphrased (iron already metal, no extraction from ore); re-solved blind, D only
'more than a millennium before iron smelting is known ... anywhere' softened to 'long before' (the source gives mid-second-millennium smelting)
source replaced with a report of Rehren et al. 2013 that states nickel content, hammered sheets rolled into tubes
review.source_checked: Sci.News on Rehren et al. 2013 (JAS): Gerzeh beads about 3200 BC hammered from meteorites rather than ore, high nickel, thin sheets rolled into tubes, smelting much later

band7.why: Two steps (date plus nickel point to a meteorite; a meteorite arrives as metal and the bead was hammered from a fragment, so no extraction); A needs both date and nickel, B and C keep the meteorite and break on timing or on inference about the makers. Band 6.

items.subtype: T1 conditional from two cases with opposite outcomes
items.passage: Many bat species forage at night along hedgerows and other linear landscape features, such as tree lines, which also serve as commuting routes between the roosts where they spend the day and their feeding grounds. Streetlights attract insects, and fast-flying bats that catch insects in flight often feed around them, taking advantage of the concentrated prey. But when ecologist Emma Stone and colleagues installed lights that mimicked streetlights along hedgerows that lesser horseshoe bats—considerably slower fliers—used as commuting routes, far fewer bats traveled along the illuminated hedgerows, and the bats began commuting later in the evening, suggesting that the expansion of street lighting ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: affects bats mainly by changing where the insects they eat are found.
may benefit some bat species while harming others, depending on traits such as how quickly each species flies.
harms all bat species alike, since even the bats that feed near lights are drawn away from the routes they would otherwise use.
is likely to increase the number of insects available to lesser horseshoe bats along the hedgerows they use.
items.explanation: Fast-flying bats feed around streetlights, which gather their insect prey, while the slower lesser horseshoe bats avoided lit commuting routes and set out later. Street lighting can therefore help some species and harm others, with the difference tied to traits such as flight speed, as B says.

A.why_wrong: That fits the fast-flying bats that feed at streetlights, but the lesser horseshoe bats were affected because they avoided the lit routes they commute along and set out later, which the text never ties to where insects gather.

C.why_wrong: The text says fast-flying bats feed on the insects that gather at streetlights, so street lighting does not harm every species.

D.why_wrong: Lights may draw insects, but lesser horseshoe bats largely stopped using the lit hedgerows, so they would not benefit from those insects.

sources.what: University of Bristol 2009 (Stone, Jones, Harris, Current Biology): lights mimicking streetlights along hedgerows used as flight routes by lesser horseshoe bats; the slow-flying bats avoided the lit hedgerows; fast-flying bats that catch insects on the wing often feed around streetlights (the abstract adds the sharp fall in activity and delayed commuting)

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology, light pollution). S7: two cases, opposite outcomes, so the effect depends on the species. Pipistrelles and low flight dropped (not in the source); the experiment's lights named as streetlight mimics. Distractors: CAUSE (all effects run through insects: true of the fast bats only; replaces a placement option the two cases confounded), EXT, MIX (insects benefit the wrong species).

fixes: writer flag: pipistrelles by name and 'travel low to the ground' are not in the source; background narrowed to the Bristol release (fast-flying bats that catch insects on the wing feed around streetlights; slow-flying lesser horseshoe bats avoid lit hedgerows), experimental lights named as streetlight mimics

A (lights on hedgerows versus open roads) had a foothold because the two cases differ in place as well as species; rebuilt as a rival mechanism (every effect runs through where insects gather, true of the fast bats only); re-solved blind, B only
passage lengthened toward the models' median
review.source_checked: University of Bristol 2009 release on Stone, Jones, Harris (Current Biology): lights along hedgerow flight routes of lesser horseshoe bats, bats avoided lit hedgerows; fast-flying bats feed around streetlights; abstract: activity fell sharply, commuting delayed

band7.why: Two cases with opposite outcomes generalised to a species-dependent effect; A holds for the fast bats and fails for the horseshoe bats, D keeps the insects and gives them to the wrong species, C an overreach. Band 6.

items.subtype: T1 revised view after dated finds
items.passage: Until the 1970s, archaeologists generally maintained that agriculture in eastern North America originated when maize cultivation spread northward from Mexico. Later analyses of plant remains from archaeological sites in Illinois, however, identified seeds of goosefoot, sunflower, marsh elder, and squash with characteristics of domestication, such as larger seeds or thinner seed coats than their wild relatives possess, in deposits dated to about 1800 BCE. Maize, by contrast, did not reach the region until roughly 200 BCE and became a dominant crop only centuries afterward. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: maize was domesticated in eastern North America before it was grown in Mexico.
the peoples of eastern North America had no contact with peoples of Mexico before 200 BCE.
people in eastern North America developed farming on their own, well before maize arrived from the south.
goosefoot and marsh elder were more productive crops in eastern North America than maize was after it arrived from Mexico.
items.explanation: Domesticated local plants appear in Illinois around 1800 BCE, more than a thousand years before maize arrived from Mexico. Farming there therefore did not depend on maize from the south; people in the region domesticated plants on their own first, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text says maize reached the region from Mexico around 200 BCE, so it was not domesticated in eastern North America first.

B.why_wrong: The finds show only that local farming began without maize; they say nothing about whether the two regions had any contact.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares how productive these crops were; maize later became a major crop, which if anything points the other way.

sources.what: Eastern Agricultural Complex: goosefoot, sunflower, marsh elder and squash domesticated at the Riverton Site, Illinois, about 1800 BCE; eastern North America an independent center of domestication; archaeologists earlier thought farming came from Mexico; maize arrived about 200 BCE (Smith 2006 cited)

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. S11: received view (farming arrived with maize from Mexico), dated counterevidence (local domesticates 1800 BCE vs maize 200 BCE), revision. Distractors: REV, EXT, CMP.

review.source_checked: Wikipedia Eastern Agricultural Complex: earlier view of farming from Mexico with maize; Riverton, Illinois, about 1800 BCE goosefoot, sunflower, marsh elder, squash with larger seeds and thinner coats; maize about 200 BCE

items.subtype: T1 revised view: what a fuller record implies about an earlier account
items.passage: Histories of American filmmaking have often characterized screenwriting in Hollywood’s early decades as a predominantly male profession, partly because writers’ names rarely appeared on screen at the time. Copyright registrations at the Library of Congress, which were required to identify each film’s writer, present a different picture: according to these documents, roughly half of all American films written before 1925 were written by women, including Frances Marion, who was credited with more than one hundred produced films. These records suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: accounts based mainly on the credits shown on screen may understate how much early films owed to women writers.
women wrote most of the films that were popular with audiences in the years before 1925.
studios deliberately left writers’ names off the screen in order to conceal how many of their films had been written by women.
the share of American films written by women continued to grow in the years after 1925.
items.explanation: The view that early screenwriting was mostly male rested partly on screen credits, which seldom named writers. Copyright records, which had to name them, show that women wrote about half of early films, so histories that relied on what appeared on screen may have missed much of women’s work, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The records show that women wrote about half of all films, not most of them, and they say nothing about which films were popular.

C.why_wrong: The text says writers’ names in general rarely appeared on screen; it gives no reason to think the practice was aimed at hiding women’s work.

D.why_wrong: The records described cover films written before 1925; the text says nothing about what happened afterward.

sources.what: 'Half of all films written before 1925 were written by women, but writers' names rarely appeared on the screen'; the figure comes from Library of Congress copyright records, which had to list writers; Marion credited with over 130 produced films

items.notes: Area: humanities (film history). S11: received view (a male profession) based on screen credits; counterevidence from copyright records; revision. Opens on how histories were written, not on a 'pioneer' frame. Distractors: EXT, CAUSE, FUT.

review.source_checked: Wikipedia Frances Marion: half of all films written before 1925 were written by women, from Library of Congress copyright records that listed writers; writers rarely named on screen; Marion over 130 produced films

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a copying mechanism applied to a passage
items.passage: Before the invention of printing, every copy of a text was produced by hand, and a scribe transcribing a manuscript repeatedly had to look away from the exemplar to write. Returning to the exemplar, he searched for the last word he had transcribed; if that identical word also appeared a line or two farther down, his eye could settle on the later occurrence instead. Textual scholars designate the resulting error homeoteleuton, from a Greek term meaning “similar ending.” In a passage where two neighboring lines end with the same word, a handwritten copy is therefore especially likely to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: repeat one of the two lines, since the scribe would copy the same ending twice.
leave out the words that came between the two identical endings.
misspell the repeated word, since the scribe would be unsure which occurrence to follow.
match the original more closely than other passages do, since the repeated word helps the scribe keep his place.
items.explanation: If the scribe’s eye returns to the second occurrence of the word rather than the first, he resumes copying after the second one and never copies what lay between them. A passage with two nearby lines ending in the same word is therefore likely to lose the words between them, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text describes the eye landing on the later occurrence, which skips text forward; repeating a line would require the eye to jump back.

C.why_wrong: The error described concerns where the scribe resumes copying, not how he spells the word.

D.why_wrong: The repeated word is what makes the error possible, so such passages are more likely, not less likely, to be copied wrongly.

sources.what: Homeoteleuton: a scribe looking for the last word he copied may find the same word on a later line and omit a line or two; the error is passed on to later copies

items.notes: Area: humanities (manuscript studies, textual criticism). S2: the eye-skip mechanism applied to a passage with repeated line endings. Distractors: REV (dittography), OUT, REV.

items.subtype: T1 conclusion from a comparison of plots differing in species number
items.passage: Ecologists have long debated whether ecosystems containing many species are more stable than those containing few. At the Cedar Creek reserve in Minnesota, David Tilman and John Downing had been monitoring approximately two hundred grassland plots that varied widely in plant species richness when a severe drought, the most serious in roughly fifty years, struck the region in the summer of 1988. Comparing the aboveground plant biomass in each of the plots before and during the drought, the researchers determined that plots with greater species richness lost a substantially smaller proportion of their biomass than did plots with fewer species. This finding suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: grasslands with many plant species tend to receive more rainfall than grasslands with few species do.
a grassland that contains many plant species is unlikely to lose any of its biomass during a drought.
droughts reduce the number of plant species in a grassland more than they reduce its total biomass.
having a greater variety of plant species may help grassland vegetation withstand periods of drought.
items.explanation: All the plots went through the same drought, and the ones with more plant species lost a smaller share of their biomass. That points to plant diversity helping a grassland hold up during drought, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The plots shared the same drought; the text gives no sign that the diverse plots received more rain, and the comparison concerns how plots responded to the same conditions.

B.why_wrong: The diverse plots lost a smaller share of their biomass, not none of it.

C.why_wrong: The study compared biomass losses; the text reports nothing about changes in the number of species during the drought.

sources.what: Tilman, Downing 1994, Nature 367 (Cedar Creek): primary productivity in more diverse plant communities was more resistant to, and recovered more fully from, a major drought

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology). S1: plots differ in species number; same drought; biomass loss differs, so diversity may confer drought resistance. Distractors: REV of cause, EXT, VAR.

fixes: drought year narrowed to 1988 (secondary sources give 1988)
source replaced with the UMN abstract (memory note removed)
review.source_checked: UMN Experts abstract (Tilman, Downing 1994): productivity in more diverse plant communities more resistant to, and recovered more fully from, a major drought

items.subtype: T5 evidential status: a present color undercut by a known change
items.passage: Smalt, a pigment produced by grinding blue cobalt glass, was widely employed by European artists of the Renaissance and Baroque periods. Conservation scientists have established that smalt has discolored in numerous oil paintings from those periods, although not in frescoes, frequently leaving passages that were originally blue looking grayish. Some viewers of a seventeenth-century oil landscape whose sky was painted with smalt have concluded from its dull gray appearance that the artist intended to depict an overcast day. The sky’s present coloration, however, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: proves that the artist intended the sky to be a bright blue rather than gray.
would be difficult to explain if the artist had not meant to depict an overcast day.
is not conclusive evidence of how the artist meant the sky to look.
suggests that the landscape was first painted as a fresco and later copied in oil.
items.explanation: Smalt in oil paintings often turns gray over time, so a gray sky painted with smalt might once have been blue. Its present color could reflect the artist’s intent or later discoloration, so it does not settle what the artist meant, as C says.

A.why_wrong: Discoloration makes an originally blue sky possible, not certain; the artist may still have painted an overcast sky.

B.why_wrong: The discoloration of smalt in oil offers an easy explanation for a gray sky whatever the artist intended.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions frescoes only to say smalt has not discolored in them; nothing suggests this landscape began as a fresco.

sources.what: Smalt, ground cobalt glass, used by European painters from the fifteenth century; known to have discolored in oil paintings but not in fresco
National Gallery, London: degraded smalt in oil loses its colour and the paint appears brownish-grey

items.notes: Area: humanities (art history, conservation science). S5: evidence for a reading (gray sky = overcast) plus a rival account (smalt discolors in oil), so not conclusive. The landscape is a generic example, not a named work. Gray as the usual result of discoloration is general conservation knowledge. Distractors: EXT, REV, MIX.

fixes: added a National Gallery source for the grey appearance of degraded smalt in oil (colourlex states oil but not fresco discoloration only)

items.subtype: T5 negative frame: what a material analysis casts doubt on
items.passage: In 1936 a shop clerk discovered a brass plate near San Francisco Bay inscribed with a claim to the surrounding territory for England’s Queen Elizabeth I and dated 1579, the year the navigator Francis Drake is documented to have landed on the coast of present-day California. Metallurgical tests in the 1970s, however, revealed that the plate’s brass had been flattened by modern rolling equipment rather than hammered by hand and contained considerably more zinc and fewer impurities than sixteenth-century English brass. These results undermine the claim that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the plate had been left by members of Drake’s expedition.
the plate had been made by someone other than Drake’s crew.
Drake had landed on the California coast in 1579.
the plate’s inscription imitated the wording of official English documents of the 1500s.
items.explanation: Rolled brass with that much zinc and so few impurities matches modern metal, not the brass the English made in the 1500s. A plate made of modern brass could not have been left by Drake’s crew in 1579, so the tests cast doubt on that idea, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The tests support the idea that someone other than Drake’s crew made the plate; they do not cast doubt on it.

C.why_wrong: The tests concern the plate only; the text says Drake is known to have landed on the coast, and nothing about the plate’s metal bears on that.

D.why_wrong: The tests examined the metal, not the wording of the inscription, so they say nothing about whether its language imitated English documents.

sources.what: Drake's Plate of Brass: found again in 1936 by shop clerk Beryle Shinn; Bolton announced it authentic in 1937; later tests showed it was rolled by modern equipment, not hammered, with too much zinc and too few impurities for Elizabethan English brass

items.notes: Area: history. S3 with a negative frame ('casting doubt on the idea that') so the lead-in and key differ from the Vinland Map model. Distractors: POL (what the evidence supports), EXT (the landing), OUT (Bolton's method).

review.source_checked: Wikipedia Drake's Plate of Brass: found 1936 by shop clerk Beryle Shinn; 1970s tests: rolled by modern equipment, too much zinc and too few impurities for Elizabethan brass

items.subtype: T1 conditional from two cases with opposite effects on scores
items.passage: In Denmark, students aged roughly eight to fifteen complete national standardized tests on computers at times determined by their schools’ schedules, which vary for reasons unrelated to the students themselves. Analyzing approximately two million of these tests, economist Hans Henrik Sievertsen and colleagues found that performance declined with each additional hour later in the day that a test was administered. However, students who had a break of twenty to thirty minutes immediately before testing outperformed students tested at the same hour without one, by more than enough to offset an hour’s decline. Thus, a student’s score on such a test may ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: depend more on the subject being tested than on the time of day at which the test is taken.
be lowered by testing later in the day, though less so if the student has just had a break.
be unaffected by the time of day as long as the school schedules a break at some point during the day.
improve as the school day goes on, since students grow more comfortable with the testing computers.
items.explanation: Scores fell with each later hour, but a break of twenty to thirty minutes right before the test raised them by more than an hour’s decline. So testing later tends to lower a score, and a recent break reduces that effect, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The study compared times of day and breaks; the text says nothing about differences between subjects.

C.why_wrong: The break that helped came just before testing, and the text never says that a break eliminates the effect of the time of day.

D.why_wrong: The text says scores declined, not improved, as the day went on.

sources.what: Sievertsen, Gino, Piovesan 2016, PNAS: all two million Danish national tests 2009/10 to 2012/13, children aged 8 to 15; each hour later lowers performance by 0.9% of an SD; a 20 to 30 minute break raises it by 1.7% of an SD, more than the hourly decline

items.notes: Area: social science (education research). S7: two cases (later hour lowers scores; a break raises them), so the effect is conditional. Distractors: VAR, EXT, REV.

fixes: source replaced with the PMC full text (memory note removed)
review.source_checked: PMC (Sievertsen, Gino, Piovesan 2016): all two million Danish tests, ages 8 to 15, 0.9% SD lower per hour, a 20 to 30 minute break adds 1.7% SD, larger than the hourly decline

items.subtype: T4 purpose of a behavior given how a resource renews
items.passage: Bumblebees collect nectar from hundreds of individual flowers during a single foraging expedition, and each visit consumes considerable time and energy. A foraging bumblebee often alights on a blossom for only a moment and then departs without feeding. Researchers have discovered that a bumblebee visiting a flower leaves behind a faint scent mark, and that subsequent bumblebees tend to reject flowers bearing this mark until the scent dissipates. Because a flower replenishes its nectar only gradually after a visitor has depleted it, the bees’ tendency to avoid freshly marked flowers most likely serves to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: keep bees from different colonies from competing with one another for the same patch of flowers.
help bees find their way back to the flowers that have given them the most nectar in the past.
spare bees the effort of probing blossoms that are likely to hold little nectar at the moment.
protect flowers from damage that frequent visits by bumblebees could cause to their petals.
items.explanation: A fresh scent mark shows that a bee has just visited the flower, and a flower that has just been drained refills its nectar only slowly. By skipping marked flowers, a bee avoids spending time on blossoms that probably have little to offer yet, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text explains the habit through how slowly nectar refills, not through competition between colonies, and it never mentions colonies.

B.why_wrong: The marks make bees avoid flowers, not return to them; bees reject marked flowers rather than seeking them out.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about damage to petals; the reason it gives concerns the nectar a flower holds after a visit.

sources.what: In at least some species, a bumblebee that has visited a flower leaves a scent mark on it, which deters bumblebees from visiting that flower until the scent degrades

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior, pollination). S9: a behavior (rejecting marked flowers) plus a stated condition (slow nectar refill) reveals its purpose. Distractors: CAUSE (competition), REV (marks attract), OUT (petal damage).

review.source_checked: Wikipedia Bumblebee: a visitor leaves a scent mark that deters other bumblebees until it degrades

items.subtype: T1 conclusion: a signal changes light quality but not quantity
items.passage: Green leaves absorb most of the red light that reaches them but reflect a substantial portion of the far-red light, a band of wavelengths just beyond the range of human vision. Ecologist Carlos Ballaré and colleagues discovered that seedlings growing near other plants receive additional far-red light reflected from neighboring leaves well before those neighbors begin to shade them, and that the seedlings respond by elongating their stems. Since the reflected light alters the composition of the light a plant receives without reducing the quantity available to it, these findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: young plants lengthen their stems mainly in response to a drop in the total amount of light they receive.
far-red light supplies the energy that young plants use to lengthen their stems.
young plants growing alone lengthen their stems faster than young plants growing near neighbors do.
plants can detect nearby competitors before those competitors begin to block their light.
items.explanation: The young plants responded to far-red light reflected from neighbors at a stage when the neighbors were not yet shading them, and that light did not reduce the light available to them. So the plants sensed their neighbors through the change in wavelengths before any competition for light had begun, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The text says the stems lengthened while the amount of light available was unchanged, so a drop in total light cannot explain the response.

B.why_wrong: The text presents reflected far-red light as information about neighbors, not as a source of energy; leaves reflect it rather than absorb it.

C.why_wrong: The plants near neighbors were the ones that lengthened their stems in response to the reflected light, not plants growing alone.

sources.what: Ballaré, Scopel, Sánchez 1990, Science, abstract: seedlings moved among plants of similar stature lengthened their stems within 3 days, well before shading among neighbors became important; the response was reduced or abolished when stems were blinded to far-red light scattered by the neighbors

items.notes: Area: natural science (plant biology). S6: the neighbors change the light's wavelengths but not its amount, so the response signals neighbors before competition. Older study (1990), kept for a plant-science spread. Distractors: REV, CAUSE (energy), REV.

fixes: 'well before those neighbors are tall enough to shade them' changed to 'begin to shade them' (the neighbors were of similar stature)
source replaced with the PubMed abstract (memory note removed)
review.source_checked: PubMed abstract (Ballaré, Scopel, Sánchez 1990): stem elongation within 3 days among similar-sized plants, well before shading, reduced when stems were blinded to far-red light scattered by neighbors

items.subtype: T6 function: what a scribe's habit was for
items.passage: Medieval books were assembled from gatherings, small stacks of folded sheets that were written on separately and later sewn together. A scribe often wrote a catchword at the bottom of the last page of a gathering. The catchword was identical to the first word on the first page of the next gathering. Gatherings were often stored or handled loose for some time before a bookbinder finally sewed them together into a volume. Scribes most likely added catchwords so that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: a binder could check that the gatherings were being sewn together in the right order.
readers could find a particular passage quickly by looking up its first word.
scribes could keep track of how many words they had copied each day.
a gathering whose first page had been damaged or lost could still be read from beginning to end.
items.explanation: Each catchword repeats the first word of the next gathering, and the gatherings sat loose until a binder sewed them together. Matching each catchword to the next gathering’s first word would let the binder confirm the order, as A says.

B.why_wrong: Catchwords appear only at the end of each gathering and repeat the next gathering’s first word, so they would not help readers find passages.

C.why_wrong: A single word at the end of a gathering could not serve as a count of words copied; the text links catchwords to the next gathering.

D.why_wrong: A catchword preserves only one word, so it could not replace a damaged page; the text never mentions damage.

sources.what: A catchword at the foot of a handwritten or printed page anticipates the first word of the following page and helped binders make sure the leaves were bound in the right order

items.notes: Area: humanities (book history). S9 easy: a practice reveals its purpose. Distractors: OUT, CAUSE, OUT.

review.source_checked: Wikipedia Catchword: anticipates the first word of the next page, helped the binder bind the leaves in the right order

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a dispersal trait in a new setting
items.passage: Many plants in the daisy family, such as hairy cat’s ear, produce seeds attached to tufts of fine hairs. These tufts function like parachutes, so the wind can transport the seeds a long distance. On the mainland, this is an advantage, because the seeds can reach unoccupied ground far from the parent plant. Ecologists Martin Cody and Jacob Overton studied plants like these on small islands off the coast of British Columbia, Canada. On such an island, a plant whose seeds travel far on the wind would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: spread its seeds to more places than the same kind of plant could on the mainland.
lose many of its seeds to the water that surrounds the island.
produce fewer flowers than the same kind of plant does on the mainland.
attract more insects to its flowers than plants with heavier seeds do.
items.explanation: Seeds that the wind carries a long way reach open ground on the mainland, but a small island is surrounded by water. Many of the seeds that blow far from a plant on such an island would end up in the water, as B says.

A.why_wrong: A small island offers little land in any direction, so seeds that travel far would mostly leave the island rather than reach more places on it.

C.why_wrong: The text is about how far seeds travel, not about how many flowers the plants produce.

D.why_wrong: The text never discusses insects or how they are attracted to flowers.

sources.what: Cody, Overton 1996, Journal of Ecology, abstract: wind-dispersed plants on inshore islands of British Columbia lost dispersal potential within a few generations, consistent with strong selection for reduced dispersal on islands (Hypochaeris radicata among them)

items.notes: Area: natural science (evolutionary ecology). S2 easy: wind dispersal applied to a small island. The key stops at the immediate consequence (seeds lost to water), one step short of the study's evolutionary finding. Distractors: REV, OUT, OUT.

fixes: source replaced with the Europe PMC record of the abstract (memory note removed); the europepmc.org page refuses scripted fetches, so the REST record URL is cited
review.source_checked: Cody, Overton 1996 abstract: wind-dispersed plants of inshore British Columbia islands lost dispersal potential within a few generations, consistent with strong selection against dispersal on islands

items.subtype: T4 explanation: a product moved from one place but not another
items.passage: In the mid-2010s, several large supermarket chains in the United Kingdom stopped displaying sweets, chocolate, and crisps at their checkouts, where shoppers stand in line waiting to pay. The policies covered only what was displayed at the checkouts, so shoppers could still buy the same snacks elsewhere in the store. Public health researcher Katrine Ejlerskov and her colleagues compared the purchases recorded by thousands of households at these supermarkets before and after the changes. They found that shoppers bought about 17 percent fewer small packages of these snacks to take home. This finding suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: shoppers came to prefer crisps over sweets and chocolate after the checkouts were changed.
supermarkets earned more money after removing snacks from their checkouts.
many of these snacks had been bought because they were in view while shoppers waited to pay.
shoppers at supermarkets without such policies bought more snacks from the aisles than from the checkouts.
items.explanation: The policies changed only what was displayed at the checkouts, and the same snacks could still be bought elsewhere in the store. Since purchases dropped anyway, many of them must have been prompted by seeing the snacks while waiting to pay, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text reports fewer purchases of all three kinds of snack together; it says nothing about shoppers preferring one kind over another.

B.why_wrong: The study measured what shoppers bought, not how much money the supermarkets made.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no information about where shoppers at other supermarkets bought their snacks.

sources.what: Ejlerskov et al. 2018, PLOS Medicine: supermarket checkout food policies associated with an immediate 17.3% reduction in purchases of small packages of common checkout foods (sugary confectionery, chocolate, crisps)

items.notes: Area: social science (public health, consumer behavior). S6 easy: snacks removed from checkouts but not from aisles; purchases fell, so checkout display drove impulse buys. Distractors: OUT, OUT, CMP.
